text.p: The ethics controversy that has clouded his future as speaker of the U.S. House of Representatives did not stop Newt Gingrich on Saturday from prescribing a "moral purpose" for America in the next century.

After a topsy-turvy week that saw him re-elected speaker by only a narrow margin, the embattled conservative returned home to Georgia for a spurt of weekend appearances on behalf of a private charity and an environmental land trust.

His first stop was a Habitat for Humanity fund-raiser at a local high school, where he preached about the virtues of volunteerism, self-reliance and religious faith to about 200 white suburbanites and their teenage children.
"This is the great moral purpose of America in the 21st century: to first heal ourselves and then to help heal the entire human race," the Republican speaker said.
"If 250 million people do a few good things, the 16 million who need help the most will be drowned in love and care and affection. It'll work."

Like the college lectures at the centre of his ethics case, Saturday's speech conveyed a vision of America in which everyone -- black and white, rich and poor -- learns to pull himself up by his own bootstraps. "We are beginning a new conversation," Gingrich told his audience.

"Every one of us who is white should reach out a helping hand to every American who is not white. At the same time, every person who is not white has an obligation to open their heart a little bit to the possibility that we are all Americans and that racism is not the core of our development."

The only things the press wanted to hear about, however, were his ethics problems and a taped cellular phone discussion in which he was reported to have talked to other Republican leaders about how to handle the ethics issue after promising a House subcommittee that he would not to do so.

A poll by Newsweek magazine to appear on Monday found that almost half of all Americans (49 percent) think Gingrich should step down as speaker because his ability to lead the Republican party has been seriously compromised.

The poll showed a third of Republicans (33 percent) and nearly two-thirds of Democrats (64 percent) think Gingrich should give up the speakership right away. The telephone poll of 753 adults conducted Jan. 9-10 has a 4 percentage points margin of error.
"I think we're off to a great start," Gingrich cheerfully told the two-dozen reporters who swarmed his every step to ask about the events of the past week in Washington.

"(Tuesday's) speech was well-received -- we got four standing ovations. I have had a number of Democrats tell me they are delighted and look forward to working with us ... and I think all that other stuff will just work itself out."
When pressed further on the ethics issue, the 53-year-old Georgia Republican retreated into a mantra of "no comments."

Later, he confessed to a local television reporter that he did not own a cellular phone. No one asked about the one he was pictured speaking into in a news photo published on Wednesday by the New York Times.
The cellphone issue erupted late in the week as Republicans and Democrats traded accusations over a shortened timeframe for the end-game of Gingrich's ethics case.
